methods.what: Police-reported crashes from CCRS (CHP), all severities including property damage only. Deleted reports dropped; the newest report version kept; preliminary reports flagged.
cite: Sec. 2.1: SWITRS/CCRS as the statewide crash repository

methods.what: Default: the last 5 finalized years. A year is treated as final once 18 months have passed since it ended (CHP data entry lags 12-18 months), so in October 2026 the default ends on 2024. The engineer can choose 1-10 years and later years; under 3 years the app warns. Windows that include 2020 or 2021 carry a COVID note.
cite: Sec. 2, p. 14: at least 3, preferably 5 years
Ch. 10: typically three to five years
CHP data entry lags 12-18 months; 2025 and later provisional

methods.what: Each crash counted once at its most severe outcome: K fatal, A suspected serious, B suspected minor, C possible, O property damage only. Injury crashes with no reported level are kept as a separate level (U) and disclosed.

A crash within 250 ft of a study intersection's center is assigned to that intersection; when two intersections compete, the nearest wins. Other crashes within the corridor buffer go to the segment they fall in.
cite: Sec. 2: crashes within 250 ft of an intersection center are attributed to it; closest intersection when centers are under 500 ft apart
Part C, Sec. C.6.2: intersection vs. segment crashes

methods.what: Segments run from intersection center to intersection center; this is the length used for per-mile figures and segment rates.
cite: Part C, Sec. C.6.2: a segment begins and ends at the center of an intersection

methods.what: Crashes CHP flags as freeway (IsFreeway) are excluded from an arterial study and reported by rule. Ramp-terminal studies can include them with a switch on the Corridor step.
Shown only where AADT is entered. Intersections: crashes per million entering vehicles (MEV = entering vehicles per day x 365 x years / 10^6). Segments: crashes per 100 million vehicle-miles.

Entered by the engineer for the project (no automatic source). Either daily two-way AADT, or two-way peak-hour volumes converted with a K factor: AADT = peak-hour volume / K, with K = 10% by default (typical; the engineer can set 4-25%). The report states which basis and K were used.
cite: K = percentage of AADT during the peak hour, both directions

methods.what: The engineer enters two-way AADT for the major and minor road. Total entering volume = major + minor at a 4-leg intersection and major + minor/2 at a T (the minor road enters from one side only). Leg count comes from OpenStreetMap and the engineer can change it.
cite: Ch. 4, Eq. 4-2: TEV = total entering vehicles per day

methods.what: Where 3 or more similar locations have AADT, each location's rate is compared with its critical rate at 95% confidence: average rate of the corridor's own intersections (or segments) + K·√(average rate / exposure) + 1 / (2 × exposure), K = 1.645. Locations above it are flagged. Statewide TASAS averages for state highways are decided (#34 item 7) but not built yet.
cite: Ch. 4, Sec. 4.2.3: critical rate from the average rate at similar sites
critical rate = average rate + K·√(average rate / exposure) + 1 / (2 × exposure), K = 1.645 at 95%
Sec. 3.1, p. 23: compare with similar areas around the state

methods.what: Decided for corridors on the State Highway System (#34 item 7): compare with Caltrans TASAS average rates by rate group. Not built yet; needs the Caltrans average-rate tables as a data source.
cite: Sec. 3.1, p. 23: compare with similar areas around the state

methods.what: Excess proportion of specific crash types: each location compared with locations of the same kind on the corridor (intersections with intersections, segments with segments), HSM variance and beta prior, ranked by excess proportion. A binomial test is used, and labelled, when the reference group is too small. Darkness is split into 'under street lights' and 'without working street lights'. The report states how many tests ran, since a few patterns can pass by chance at P ≥ 0.80.
cite: Ch. 4, Sec. 4.2.3 and 4.4.2: excess proportions of specific crash types
Ch. 10: only similar location types analyzed together
high-proportion screening; P = 1 - betadist(p*, a + x, b + n - x)

methods.what: A draft pattern library from the HSM diagnosis step, labelled draft until the engineer approves it (#34 item 6).
cite: Ch. 10: collision diagrams and pattern identification

methods.what: Not built (#52). Weight = crash cost of the severity / PDO crash cost; FHWA publishes current KABCO crash costs.
CrashIQ is a site (hot-spot) analysis of one corridor; the findings name crash types that systemic countermeasures also target.
cite: Sec. 1.6: combine spot and systemic approaches

methods.what: Intersections and traffic control come from OpenStreetMap; the engineer reviews and edits them on the Corridor step.

A report without usable GPS is placed from its two street names on the OpenStreetMap network, at the intersection, then moved by the report's distance and direction along the primary road. It is placed automatically when both names match exactly, or when the two streets can meet at only one place allowing only what the report leaves out (a leading or trailing direction, a suffix: AVENUE J & 20TH ST W is West Avenue J & 20th Street West). A direction the report writes must match. Pairs that meet in more than one place, and looser matches, go to the review list. User decisions 2026-10-18 (exact, 98% bar) and 2026-10-22 (unique pair).

methods.topic: Police GPS vs the report's description
methods.what: GPS at the intersection the report names (within 50 ft), when the report states a distance over 50 ft and a direction, is moved to that intersection plus the distance, along the named road (provenance gps_offset_applied). GPS on a default or dispatch point (one exact point, to 5 decimals, shared by 10 or more reports naming 5 or more street pairs, under half of which it fits; pooled across agencies, from a statewide scan of CCRS 2021-25) or written with 2 decimals or fewer (about 1 km) in both coordinates, or in one where the point doesn't fit the report's streets, is not a location: the report is placed by its street names, and reports whose GPS sits on such a point elsewhere are found by name too. Wrong-format (degrees-minutes-seconds) GPS is converted. User decision 2026-10-22.

Crashes are placed, and report street names checked, on OpenStreetMap joined with the US Census TIGER/Line roads of the counties the corridor is in. A TIGER road running along an OpenStreetMap street (most of its length within 12 m) adds its names to that street; a TIGER road OpenStreetMap lacks is added and joined at the nearest OpenStreetMap corner. Each street keeps where its name comes from (OpenStreetMap, TIGER or both); a crash placed with a name or road only TIGER/Line has is marked, and one that needs a road only TIGER/Line has goes to the review list as a suggestion until its accuracy is measured statewide. User decisions 2026-10-22 and 2026-10-24 (on statewide; roads only TIGER has stay suggestions).

methods.topic: Correcting small typos in street names
methods.what: A report name with no exact or one-place match is corrected to a map street only when it isn't a guess: at most 2 character edits (1 for names of 4 letters or fewer; a swap of two neighbouring letters counts as one), never a change of digits, no other street within the same number of edits or one more, the corrected pair of streets meeting at exactly one intersection, and police GPS, where the crash has it, within 400 ft (plus the stated offset) of that corner. Until the accuracy is measured on hidden police GPS and the user approves, such a crash is a suggestion on the review list (user decision 2026-10-22, #233).

Some cities' reports spell a street their own way (MARTIN LUTHER KING JR WY for Martin Luther King Junior Way in Oakland). A table of such spellings, each with its evidence and approved by the user one by one, is applied in its own city only: the report's street name is read as the map street's name in every check and placement, the name as reported is kept, and each crash lists the entries used. Entries not approved are never used. User decisions 2026-10-22.

A freeway report names the freeway (or a ramp, or a connector 'X TO Y'), a reference street that usually crosses over or under it, and a distance and compass direction from it, read as written. Mainline: from where the reference street crosses the lanes of the stated travel direction, the stated distance along those lanes. Ramp: at the ramp terminal on the reference street (under 400 ft), else along the ramp. Connector: from where it reaches the second freeway, the stated distance along the connector. A description that fits more than one place is never guessed. The officer's GPS, where a crash has it, is kept as it is: moving GPS that disagrees with the report is not used (it waits for the user's decision). Since 2026-10-24 (user): a freeway crash with no usable GPS is placed this way as approximate (usually within 0.5 mi: about 95% of tested crashes), counted on segments only and left out of intersection tables and collision diagrams; officer GPS is kept as it is.

Each counted crash on a state route gets its Caltrans postmile (county-route-PM, e.g. LA-405 PM 12.345), interpolated between the two 0.1-mile postmile points that bracket where CrashIQ placed it, on the side of the stated travel direction when the report gives one. It is derived from the placement, not from CHP, and doesn't change it. User decision 2026-10-23 (#248).
